title: Selecting product metrics: a value-chain KPI system for teams, execs and stakeholders
summary: Jason Cohen proposes mapping product metrics as a value chain across time (leading to lagging) and across hidden, internal, external and strategic domains, so every department sees itself in the result. He pairs this with a checklist for good metrics, including plain-language definitions, causing action, and signal at least 2x stronger than noise.

principles.text: Map metrics as a value chain by time, actor and type of value; each box then yields its own metrics.
principles.quote: A product sits in the middle of a chain of events, executed by the team, customers, and peers across all departments.

principles.text: Separate maximizers from satisficers; act on satisficing KPIs only when they hit a pre-agreed violation threshold.
principles.quote: "satisficing" KPIs are tracked continuously, but the team acts only when a KPI slips into "violation" territory, as opposed to fielding requests to invest in improving those KPIs.

principles.text: Hold teams accountable for immediate, controllable work. Treat revenue as a lagging, multi-input outcome.
principles.quote: Work can--and should--be measured sprint-by-sprint, whereas revenue is a multi-input, lagging indicator of success.

principles.text: Measure both direct results and lagging outcomes; missing an outcome is a learning, not a failure.
principles.quote: But "not yet achieving the outcome" is not a complete failure, but rather a learning that will shape the work that will be executed in the next two weeks.

principles.text: A metric belongs on the main board only if a change would make you act; otherwise keep it operational.
principles.quote: If the answer is "no," it doesn't belong on our main metrics board.

principles.text: A KPI the team doesn't believe in will be ignored; the team must want to depend on it.
principles.quote: Whenever management requires a KPI that the team doesn't believe in, doesn't respect, doesn't care about, the team always wins.
